title: Did you know King's Lynn has centuries-old history of witch trials and spectral sightings that shape its association with Halloween today?
excerpt: With spooky season in full swing, did you know that Lynn is one of the country's most haunted market towns?
content:
But do you really know what it is all about and why it is celebrated? Well, fear not!

Although it is a celebration for many. Historically, there are creepier connections to this time of year for us here in the West Norfolk town.

With many tales to be told across the world, here in Lynn, it has a dark, centuries-old local history of witch trials, legends, and spectral sightings that shape its association with Halloween today – did you know that hundreds of years ago our very own witch was burnt at the stake?

WITCH TRIALS AND PERSECUTION IN THE TOWN

Margaret Read,​​​​​​ who was accused and then found guilty of witchcraft in the 1570s and 1580s, was burned at the stake on the Tuesday Market Place in 1590.

Numbers 15 and 16 on the marketplace are historic Grade II-listed red brick buildings on the north side of the square, famously known as the home of the ‘Witch's Heart’ carving.

Legend has it that as she was being consumed by flames, Margaret’s heart burst from her chest, smashed into the spot above the window, which is now marked with a diamond, and then fell to the ground before it beat a determined path to the nearby River Ouse, where it sank beneath the surface, the water bubbling and roiling as it was enveloped.

This is just one SPOOKY snippet the town has to offer!

HAUNTED LOCATIONS IN LYNN

True’s Yard Fisherfolk Museum is believed to be home to more than 37 resident ghosts. Visitors to the museum have witnessed many unexplainable sights over the years, including dark figures staring out of empty windows of the 18th-century cottages.

Back in 2012, a ‘ghostly’ face was captured on camera appearing through a window at the premises. The building has previously been suspected by ghost hunters as being 'haunted' for years, possibly by the souls of dead seafarers.

Staff have also reported witnessing a poltergeist, known as Henry, knocking paintings off walls and throwing staplers across a room where fisherfolk used to live.

In January this year, The Lattice House was believed to have been in the presence of a ghost after “paranormal activity” occurred.

A 27-second clip caught the moment a full glass slowly moved towards the edge of a table and then fell off.

The landlord at the time, Perry Sturge, said he was out the back at the time and had one of his staff members at the front bar when they heard an “almighty bang” at the table, which had just been vacated by a punter.

He had previously been told of numerous occasions where people have experienced “pints flying off the tables” and people ending up with “dinners on their laps”. However, he had not caught any previous experiences on camera until that occasion.

The Purfleet Quay was Lynn’s principal anchorage for ships during medieval times, and there have in the past been reports of a ghost wandering around the area, before screaming and throwing itself into the water. Ghostly screams of fighting soldiers have also been heard, and the water is said to run red with blood.

The Duke’s Head Hotel was built in 1683 and is known to be one of the most haunted buildings in the historic town of Lynn. It stands on the site of an ancient inn called the Gryffin, and the ghost of a maidservant is believed to haunt the local landmark.

According to reports, the maid was found guilty of poisoning her mistress and was sentenced to be boiled alive on the Tuesday Market Place.

Dark discoveries have also been found in the hotel. In 2011, cat remains were found in the ceiling of Room 10. Local historians believe that the cat remains were placed there to deter evil spirits and witches from entering the property.

The 16th-century former Tudor Rose Hotel is said to be home to several ghosts. A short woman wearing a wedding dress has been spotted walking around the historic hotel by visitors. The legend goes that the bride was murdered by her new husband on their wedding day. Paranormal activities include phantom footsteps, objects moving, doors closing, and mysterious shadows passing.

Known locally as the ‘Exorcist’s House’, the property, which is now a private residence on Chapel Lane, is the former home of a medieval exorcist. The last exorcism was carried out in the 16th century and is said to have led to the burning of Margaret, accused of witchcraft.

A local folktale says that the devil arrived in Lynn by ship and headed into the market town to steal the souls of the local townsfolk. However, his plan failed when a priest came upon him and cornered him in a cobbled alleyway, now called Devil’s Alley.

The priest banished him with prayers and holy water, causing the furious devil to stomp his foot so hard into the cobbles that he left an imprint of his hoof. The devil was forced back to the ship and was never to be seen again. Although the Devil’s hoofprint seems to have disappeared, this local folktale still lives on.

But where did the spooky season come from?

ORIGINS OF HALLOWEEN

The tradition dates back more than 2,000 years to the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain in Ireland and the British Isles. The Celts celebrated their new year on November 1 and believed spirits crossed over on the night of October 31.

The Celts believed that Samhain was the day in the year – that marked the end of the harvest season and the beginning of the dark, cold winter – when the boundary between our world and the spirits became thin.

If that is not SPOOKY enough for you…

To protect themselves from roaming ghosts, people lit massive bonfires and wore disguises or animal skins to trick or frighten away evil entities.

Eventually, the church created ‘All Saints' Day’ – a Christian celebration – with the night before being called ‘All Hallows' Eve’, leading to the name Halloween.

Then, over the last hundreds of years, as beliefs and cultures blended, Halloween has evolved into what it is today, with popular activities including trick-or-treating, attending Halloween costume parties, carving pumpkins, lighting bonfires, apple bobbing, playing pranks, visiting haunted attractions, telling frightening stories, and watching horror or Halloween-themed films.
